title: Death, difficulty and progression
thesis: Permadeath is not a punishment but consequence persistence: it makes choices, risks and randomness matter, and everything else in this chapter is about keeping that promise fair, fast and worth repeating. A designer should leave knowing how to make deaths feel earned, how much to soften them, how to shape randomness and clocks so the optimal play is also the fun play, and how to tune difficulty and progression for players who will start over many times.

sections.heading: Why permadeath: consequence persistence
sections.brief: Open with Glenn Wichman's reframing of permadeath as 'consequence persistence': Rogue made actions irreversible so that choices (above all unidentified items) mean something, and the good outcomes are as permanent as the bad. Then show the convergence of later talks on why that matters: bhauth's poker-with-save-and-reload argument that permadeath forces players to reason about probability, Brevik and Furmanski on the tension of a long-lived character dying to one mistake, and Moromisato's 'one more game' illusion of winnability. Set the philosophical readings (Cartlidge's confrontation with mortality, Sahin's fear without real danger, Leonhart's queer art of failure, Kreminski's attachment to a disposable generated character) beside the practical ones (Noita's destruction becoming self-balancing, Sersa Victory's point that permadeath makes players actually spend consumables). Close with droqen's 'monolithic challenge' and Julian Day's point that the run structure normalises extreme difficulty, and give the designer the test: what in your game becomes a real decision only because it cannot be undone?

sections.heading: Fair deaths and deaths that teach
sections.brief: Argue that permadeath only works when the player believes the death was theirs. Lead with the convergent definitions: Moromisato (the player always knows why they died), Aversa's Tangledeep criteria (understandable challenges, responsibility, clear effects), Alan Malloy's 'fun death has a tactical lesson', and Gillian Smith's point that failure is only fun when normalised and nameable. Then the levers for removing unfair deaths: Noita tracking 'insta-kill cleanliness', Ultimate ADOM's traps that wound rather than kill, Liotta adding undo, Chogue keeping rooms lit, bcrawl's fairness fixes, and Larsen letting players pay to skip an impossible puzzle; set against Mike Cook's alternative of designing scoring so an unfair run isn't expected to be won, and Tringali leaning into sharp punishment as the theme of The Banished Vault. Include the attrition problem (Feinberg on regeneration, Shawn Main on persistent health making easy fights matter) and the softer side of presentation (N++'s dying attract screen, Super Meat Boy's replay, Dredmor's mocking death screen, Dungeonmans' heroic deaths, the 'fair yet stupid' story death). End with practical guidance: audit every way to die for warning, counterplay and lesson.

sections.heading: The cost of starting over: restarts, run length and the early game
sections.brief: Treat the time between death and the next interesting decision as a design budget. Lead with the convergence: John Harris (time invested is the ante; make restarting painless), Lisa Brown (Nuclear Throne's five-second failure loop versus Enter the Gungeon), and Andrew Aversa's 'End of Permadeath' argument that default permadeath promises the early game will be seen many times, so it must be varied and free of a heavy opening story or permadeath should not be the default. Add Berman's rule that every run's opening should be winnable by random play, Shawn Main on distinct enforced starting positions, and Spelunky's low early penalty. Then run length as a lever: espresso, coffee-break and movie-length runs, FTL and Against the Storm setting a target length early, Slay the Spire cutting act length, Desktop Dungeons compressing a Crawl run into ten minutes, and Aversa on how run length scales the sting of loss; bring in Brown and Salzman on short horizons and short runs serving low-strategy and neurodivergent players. End with concrete guidance: measure death-to-play time, set a run-length target, and front-load variety.

sections.heading: Softening death: a spectrum of penalties
sections.brief: Start from Aversa's redefinition: optional permadeath is any mode where dying need not cost all progress, a spectrum rather than a switch, and the default mode shapes how players perceive the game. Present the evidence for offering softer modes (about 30% of Tangledeep players chose adventure mode and saw content only 2% of runs reach; Langford on children; Boyfriend Dungeon and Hades as entry tiers) and against doing it carelessly (Lab of Legends removing consequence so players got stuck; Aversa on hazards that are fair without permadeath feeling unfair with it, on save-anywhere not being easier, and on the endgame having to deliver once players expect to finish). Walk the spectrum of intermediate penalties: lives, Mystery Dungeon's collapse-and-lose-items, Dark Souls' bloodstain, Wildermyth's mortal choice between maiming and a glorious death, Roundguard's theatre reset, ghosts and revives in multiplayer, The Wandering Village's death toggle. End by stating what the choice depends on (audience, budget, run length) and Clark's warning that permanent loss thresholds differ so no one experience fits everyone.

sections.heading: Deaths that leave a mark: legacies, bones and worlds that remember
sections.brief: Present the alternative to a clean reset: deaths that feed a persistent world. Lead with Dwarf Fortress, where lost forts and adventurers stay in the world so 'losing is fun' and nothing is truly lost, then Prey: Mooncrash (five characters sharing one finite-resource world, explicitly choosing a 'Rogue Legacy model' over a stateless 'Spelunky model') and Cole Wehrle's Oath, where every end state is a valid start state and the deck shifts about 10% per game. Follow with smaller-scale legacies: Dungeonmans' pyres, bequeathed items, NetHack bones (and Adeon turning them off for speedruns), Shiren's restaurant and castle, romantic partners carrying a story, successive hordes in La Horde du Contrevent. Stage Solomons' open question of runs that accrue burdens rather than upgrades, with his own warning about frustration. End with guidance on what to persist (world state, stories, items) without it becoming power creep, handing off to the meta-progression section.

sections.heading: Meta-progression: knowledge, power and presence
sections.brief: Use Jim Shepard's framework as the spine: metaprogression is whatever survives the game-over reset, in three kinds (meta knowledge, meta power, meta presence), with meta power either kinetic or soft. Then the core disagreement: Shawn Main argues meta-progression pairs naturally with roguelikes because players want rewarding for their time, while Noita relies on 'virtual skill' (knowledge only), Keenan and Aversa warn of grind and 'I have to die to build my character', Shepard shows how too much meta power breaks early and late balance, and Liessen warns against locking in a broken state; Shiren's Wii version keeping levels is the cautionary example. Show the middle paths: Aversa's 'get through the early game faster, don't raise the ceiling', soft unlocks that only change probabilities (Dream Quest), Dungeonmans' capped carry-over and Ironman mode, pity access to new areas, randomizer knowledge, braided narratives that advance on every run, and diegetic presentation (Grimoire Groves' garden, Backpack Hero's town). Close with Gillian Smith's fractal loops (moment, room, run, meta) as the frame for deciding which loop carries progress.

sections.heading: What randomness is for
sections.brief: Make the case for randomness before taming it. Lead with Shawn Main: randomness creates variety, variety drives engagement, and games need uncertainty even if not randomness (Portal once known is done); Debenham agrees randomness makes roguelikes replayable. Then Main's key distinction between setup randomness (adaptable, novel) and results randomness (most emotional, most likely to feel like losing to dice), and how it converges with Into the Breach moving randomness to the input, Thousand Hells moving from dice to visible cards, and Andrea Roberts' point that a complex deterministic system (Roundguard's physics) is itself a source of chance. Stage the tension: Main and others value big swings and drama, John Harris warns a structureless random dungeon reduces to gambling, and the 'artful randomness' audience comment gives the test (can the player build intuition?). Add variance as an audience choice (Gavin Verhey on Magic, Main on mixed-skill play) and players' poor intuition for probability (Feinberg, Pagnutti's binomial maths). End with how to decide where randomness sits in your game.

sections.heading: Smoothing the sharp edges of RNG
sections.brief: A technique catalogue built on Evan Debenham's talk: rare extremes (miss streaks, duplicate items) make success feel luck-driven, and roguelike runs are too short for outcomes to average out, so smooth extremes while keeping excitement (and it is fine to keep RNG sharp). List the tools with their speakers and parameters: shuffled decks with no repeat at the seam, pyramid and bell distributions, forced averaging, pity timers (Debenham, Berman), Dead Cells' 'hidden game master' loot director, build-biased and re-placed legendaries, top-down gold budgets and scheduled 'golden runs' (Sébastien Benard), Brough's 'roll several and pick one', narrowed ranges and a chance to respond, his point that teleport regresses to the mean, Brogue's rubber-banded reward rooms, Star Freighter never letting the exceptional event happen first, Clash Royale's fixed hidden cycle, DiIorio's chance effects that still help when they fail, Tangledeep's tight damage ranges, randomizers restricting shuffles to key items. Close with the warning cases: Max Hawkins on rerolls defeating a randomizer, and Tyler Coleman's stock-price spawn weights as an unusual non-RNG source. Finish with a short table-like list of which tool fits which problem.

sections.heading: Push your luck: risk the player chooses
sections.brief: Argue that the best risk in a roguelike is risk the player opts into. Lead with Nic Tringali's push-your-luck framework (information and uncertainty stored and revealed through decks, dice and people) with Blackjack, Can't Stop and Skull as the contrasting cases, and Sersa Victory's agonising tradeoff as the definition of a good choice, with unidentified items, out-of-depth monsters and vaults as the classic roguelike gambles and Tarn Adams likening an accusation to reading an unknown scroll. Then techniques: Jon Perry's mitigations in Party House (long game, consolation popularity, temporary ban), The Banished Vault's unknown-cost hazards turning into a buffer meta-resource, Apocalypse World's partial-success band, Forays into Norrendrin's single rest per level, Dragon's Descent's one-pick treasure room, money-runs-out structures in Stream Heist, Nuzlocke encounter routing, and the Hobbit variant's choose-your-own-orcs scoring. End with guidance: make risk visible, voluntary, and recoverable enough to keep the player in the run.

sections.heading: When the optimal play is the boring play
sections.brief: Lead with Nicholas Feinberg's infinite-patience test: imagine a player with unlimited tolerance for tedium, and if their win-maximising use of a system is not fun, the design is broken, because unfun optimal strategies hurt even players who don't use them (they blame their deaths on skipping the grind); NetHack's pudding farming and the 'punishment is the tedium' attitude are the warning. Converge with John Harris on eliminating grind and with the Angband history: Osheim and Au on diving beating slow stair-scumming, and Nick McConnell on the community discovering that aggressive diving wins more games per hour, so development now assumes it; add the countermeasures (fuzzy detection, nerfing teleport-away play, forced descent belongs to the next section). Include smaller cases: stair scumming named, Beneath Apple Manor treasure racing, NetHack's level-generation-time monster scaling, Angband's junk problem, Wii Shiren encouraging grind, and Leonard Richardson's open question of subverting grind. End with how to detect degenerate strategies in your own design, which sets up the clocks section.

sections.heading: Clocks: hunger, timers and pressure to move on
sections.brief: Present clocks as the main answer to degenerate patience. Lead with the convergent purpose: Rosalind Miles Chapman (hunger turns time into a resource), Shawn Main (players optimise the fun out unless pushed forward), Rogue's own history (starvation added because players rested over lunch), and Feinberg's account of food clocks loosening until Crawl's is vestigial. Stage the disagreement: Tyriq Plummer removed starvation from Catacomb Kids because it punished caution and pacifism, Biskup made Ultimate ADOM hunger weaken but not kill, Caves of Qud planned to replace its system, while Aversa found Tangledeep trivial without one and attrition worse when regeneration went instead. Then the substitutes: Tangledeep's draining-and-refilling flask, Into Ruins' slowfall orb, Rift Wizard's charge-limited spells, Angband's forced descent, Spelunky's ghost, Invisible, Inc. and Castle Cthulhu's escalation, Larn's and Alphaman's deadlines, Against the Storm's stretchable Impatience meter, Sunless Sea's voyages. Include Feinberg's warnings (strong clocks punish auto-explore; fixed turn limits create 'good as dead' games; removing regeneration creates new farming exploits) and John Bond on never timing a breath moment. End with a checklist for choosing a clock.

sections.heading: Pacing a run: difficulty curves, rhythm and the endgame
sections.brief: Cover how difficulty and reward should move across a single run. Start with Everest Pipkin's observation that descent maps to rising complexity and alienness (with Gabrielaitis noting it inverts real geology), then rhythm: Pandamander's keep-rare-moments-rare and plan troughs, John Bond's 'breath' moments at doors, Animal Crossing's complementary quest pacing, and the scratch-card loop of random digging (with Pipkin's warning that such loops become Skinner boxes). Then tools for shaping a curve: Plarl's rising maximum by distance, Mooncrash building to a fever pitch, riddle chains scaling by step count and complexity, Cat Burglar's bracketed-but-shuffled questions, Paper Magic's winners-meet-winners ramp, and Keenan choosing randomness over strict ordering in Duskers. End on the endgame: NetHack's ascension escape and the annoying drag-down mechanic, Chogue testers demanding Rogue's real ending, Rogue's Gate's fetch-and-return, Mooncrash's what-not-how goals, MTG Arena's best-of-one; guidance: decide the shape of the curve and the final act before tuning numbers.

sections.heading: Power within a run: broken combos, power fantasy and variety
sections.brief: Argue that a single-player roguelike should let the player outgrow its enemies, and that the run reset is what makes this safe. Lead with Dan DiIorio (don't balance like League or chess; players have fun becoming more powerful than their enemies) and Courtney Liessen (game-breaking combos suit roguelikes because they end with the run), supported by Alice Lai on known combos letting players shape their own curve, Monster Train's deliberately wild power curve, Against the Storm ending a run quickly once the player is winning, and Desktop Dungeons turning everything into a resource for the boss. Then the counterweight: avoid dominant strategies (Pandamander's 50 versus 5,000 hours, Against the Storm rejecting city walls, Tringali destabilising the optimal route), Casey Yano's content-density tipping point, Coleman's acceptance of a shifting 80/20 meta, and Hades bounding build width. Then in-run progression forms: Tim Keenan's within-run versus between-run variety slider, item-based versus level-based progression in Backpack Hero, information as progression in The Shrouded Isle and Dwarf Fortress investigations, scarce skill points in Rift Wizard, wishes and the ascension kit, Chogue's party-as-hit-points, rarity and sets as balancing tools, and Nat Alison on order-chaos erosion over repeated play. End with guidance on where to let power spike and where to cap it.

sections.heading: Balancing with data, simulation and play
sections.brief: A methods section. Lead with Phenry Ewing's rule to decide the desired experience before simulating (even odds, hard-but-rewarding, constant near-precarity), then the three converging approaches: Jon Perry alternating feel, spreadsheets and Monte Carlo simulation (with no-strategy bots as a baseline and Party House's derived popularity cap), DCSS checking complaints against death statistics and catching a doubled-damage bug in tournament data, and simulation in Werewolf, Neo Cab and MCTS search trees mined for balance data. Stage the cautions: Berman on permadeath analytics being biased toward skilled players, Debenham on win rates confusing correlation and causation and on low-usage high-win items revealing invisible power, Backpack Hero's public nerfs drawing criticism. Then specific levers: item size, rarity, card sets, singleton pools, light sources for stealth, self-balancing contested pools, economy tuning in The Shrouded Isle's volatile stagnation, prices by fiat versus fluctuation, Cozy Grove's overpowered chair, Jeff Lait's 'wall' resources, DiIorio's tiny across-the-board buffs, The Banished Vault moving to hand-tuned values and an easier default. End with a practical balancing loop.

sections.heading: Difficulty settings and who they serve
sections.brief: Lead with Andrea Roberts (difficulty is subjective and balance never perfect, so give players tools to tune it) and Philomena Schwab (different players find different parts hard, so granular settings beat a single slider). Converge with Tangledeep's individual toggles framed as optional, Peglin's modes and Cruciball widening its streamer audience, and Luck be a Landlord resolving contradictory too-easy and too-hard feedback with 20 unlockable difficulties. Then techniques that adapt difficulty without menus: The Wandering Village's scripted-then-random easy modes, Roundguard pushing complications into the generator as players prove mastery, RimWorld's adaptive versus random storyteller, Niche's travel-direction difficulty, HyperRogue's per-land scaling, Tangledeep's Dreamcaster, revealed information as a puzzle difficulty dial, and Spelunky's layered content for different audiences. Stage the cautions: label easy modes clearly and respectfully (Roundguard's mercy relic), Lisa Brown on Ascension-style modes not motivating goal-driven players, Mike Cook on modifiers alienating daily-challenge players. End with guidance on default difficulty and how to present options.

sections.heading: Self-imposed challenge: conducts, bonus objectives and alternate rules
sections.brief: Close the chapter on players who make the game harder themselves. Lead with Kawa's definition of conduct play (deliberately changing a game's stated rules, usually to make it harder, invented by players or tracked in the game) and her advice that designers ask which mechanics are easy or hard to ignore and what high-level players altering them says about the game. Show the in-game support: NetHack's tracked conducts and Drew Streib on low-turn and high-conduct ascensions as the real feats for serial winners, ADOM's Eternium Man and extreme conducts, Hoplite's altar challenges, Shiren 5's rule-twist bonus dungeons, Heat Signature's mission clauses, Roundguard's scarab multiplier and Lab of Legends' golden wisp as optional in-fight objectives, and Slay the Spire's standard, daily and custom modes as Rabii's solid, gaseous and liquid states. Note Kawa's point that some conducts make the game easier or remove tedium, and Nat Alison on challenge runs and mods restoring a stale game. End with guidance on tracking and rewarding player-invented challenges.
